newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania scraps bank reserves cut.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania scraps bank reserves cut.

text.p: The Bank of Tanzania has scrapped a decision to cut the minimum reserves it requires commercial banks to hold, after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) expressed concern.

Bankers said on Thursday the Bank of Tanzania (BoT), the central bank, late last week amended a statement issued in December to say the Statutory Minimum Reserve would from March 1 return to its original level of 12 percent from six percent.
"Every bank is required to maintain minimum reserves equivalent to 12 percent of the outstanding balance of its total shilling deposits and borrowings from the general public," BoT said.
The BoT earlier said its December 17 decision to cut the Statutory Minimum Reserve (SMR) by 50 percent was aimed at boosting liquidity of local banks to improve savings and build private investment.
Foreign banking sources at the time said the decision was taken by the central bank without informing the IMF, which protested against the move and warned it could foil policies to reduce inflation.
IMF officials in Tanzania welcomed the decision to return to 12 percent.
"We are happy about that because we believed it was the wrong thing," IMF senior resident representative Festus Osunsade told Reuters.
Foreign bankers and economic analysts said the central bank decision to rescind such a key move marked a change in the central bank's understanding of the importance of tough economic reforms.
"It caused quite an uproar within the government because apparently the treasury, and possibly even State House, didn't even know about it," a senior economic analyst said.

"The action to revoke it indicates the concern of (President Benjamin) Mkapa's administration that all efforts should be made to keep economic reforms on track of which the ESAF (Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility) is a centrepiece," he told Reuters.
The IMF approved a $234 million ESAF package of new loans to Tanzania in November, the first new IMF support for the country since 1992.
"The important thing really is that reform is firmly on track in this country and any attempt to bring it off track will fail," said a representative of one of Tanzania's major donors.
"It demonstrates an unshaken determination. The government doesn't want to leave any doubt as to its commitment to reforms," he added.
A foreign banker said the reversal by the central bank was unlikely to dampen the confidence of local banks in the BoT.
